passages.text: Recommendation on unbiased estimation of population attributable fraction calculated in “prevalence and risk factors of active pulmonary tuberculosis among elderly people in China: a population based cross-sectional study”

Population attributable fraction (PAF) refers to the proportion of all cases with a particular outcome in a population that could be prevented by eliminating a specific exposure. <sentence_start/>The authors of a recent paper evaluated the prevalence and estimated the PAFs for risk factors of TB among elderly people in China [Inf Dis Poverty. 2019;8:7]. <sentence_start/>Confounding is inevitable in observational studies and Levin’s formula is of limited use in practice for unbiasedly estimating PAF. <sentence_start/>In a complex survey design, an unbiased estimation of the PAF can be calculated using a sample-weighted version of the Miettinen formula or a sample weighed parametric g-formula. <sentence_start/>With respect to causal interpretation of PAF in public health setting, computation of PAF is logical and practical when the exposure is amenable to intervention.
The online version of this article (10.1186/s40249-019-0587-8) contains supplementary material, which is available to authorized users.
Please see Additional file 1 for translations of the abstract into the five official working languages of the United Nations.

We read with great interest a recent article titled [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR1" doi="10.1186/s40249-019-0515-y" pmid="30654836" pmcid="PMC6337869" count="1">1</citation>]: “Prevalence and risk factors of active pulmonary tuberculosis among elderly people in China: a population based cross-sectional study”. <sentence_start/>The authors evaluated the prevalence and identify the risk factors of TB among elderly people in China using a cross-sectional study. <sentence_start/>However, there are several concerns in the analysis.

In the statistical analysis section it was indicated that population attributable fraction (PAF) of each adjusted risk factor was estimated using Levin’s formula where <italic>RR</italic> is the risk ratio and <italic>p</italic><italic><sub>e</sub></italic> means proportion of population exposed to risk factors [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR2" doi="10.1097/EDE.0000000000000177" pmid="25265137" count="1">2</citation>].
In the study, the adjusted odds ratio (<italic>OR</italic>) was used in place of <italic>RR</italic>.

PAF refers to the proportion of all cases with a particular outcome in a population that could be prevented by eliminating a specific exposure [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" doi="10.1136/bmj.k757" pmid="29472187" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Formula 1 is unbiased in the absence of confounding and effect modification [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" doi="10.1136/bmj.k757" pmid="29472187" count="1">3</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR4" doi="10.1097/EDE.0b013e3181fce49b" pmid="20975564" count="1">4</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Observational studies are subject to confounding which will lead to bias if Levin’s formula is inappropriately applied to estimate PAFs [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" doi="10.1136/bmj.k757" pmid="29472187" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The Levin’s formula is valid only for unadjusted risk ratio [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" doi="10.1136/bmj.k757" pmid="29472187" count="1">3</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5" doi="10.1097/EDE.0000000000000181" pmid="25210928" pmcid="PMC4731856" count="1">5</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The bias from this error will depend on the degree of confounding [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR6" doi="10.2105/AJPH.88.1.15" pmid="9584027" pmcid="PMC1508384" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For a dichotomous exposure an unbiased estimation of PAF can be calculated using the Miettinen’s formula [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR7" doi="10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a121617" pmid="4825599" count="1">7</citation>].

Where <italic>RR</italic><italic><sub>adj</sub></italic> is the adjusted risk ratio and <italic>p</italic><italic><sub>c</sub></italic> is the prevalence of exposure among the cases. <sentence_start/>This produces valid estimate in the presence of confounding, assuming exposure status and confounders are accurately measured and adjusted for.

As an example, in this study [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR1" doi="10.1186/s40249-019-0515-y" pmid="30654836" pmcid="PMC6337869" count="1">1</citation>] the adjusted <italic>OR</italic> and prevalence of diabetes in the active TB cases was reported 1.83 (1.08-3.10) and 16/193, respectively. <sentence_start/>The PAF using formula 2 is 3.76% which is less than the reported value (5.52%).

The term “attributable” refers to a causal interpretation [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" doi="10.1136/bmj.k757" pmid="29472187" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>One of the main assumptions underlying the PAF is no bias in study design. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the application of formula 2 in cohort design is acceptable but for case-control and cross-sectional studies, it needs more considerations. <sentence_start/>In a cross-sectional study, reverse causality and prevalence-incidence bias are the main concerns for assessing the effect of the exposure on the outcome.

Another potential source of bias in the study is failure to adjust observed estimates of the prevalence of TB and exposure to risk factors for the complex sampling design employed. <sentence_start/>With such a design, the population prevalence should be adjusted using inverse probability weighting (IPW) so that the reported prevalence is appropriately adjusted for multistage and disproportionate sampling [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8" doi="10.1136/bmj.i189" pmid="26773001" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Further, the authors do not mention whether or how clustering was taken account of in the multivariable logistic regression modeling.

For complex survey designs, it is necessary to adjust PAFs for the complex sampling design [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" doi="10.1016/j.annepidem.2014.11.007" pmid="25511308" count="1">9</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" doi="10.1111/j.1541-0420.2005.00355.x" pmid="16135037" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>PAF can be computed as a sample-weighted version of the Miettinen or Bruzzi formula (formula 2 in reference [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" doi="10.1016/j.annepidem.2014.11.007" pmid="25511308" count="1">9</citation>] or formula 3 in reference [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" doi="10.1111/j.1541-0420.2005.00355.x" pmid="16135037" count="1">10</citation>] or sample-weighted model-based standardization, also known as parametric g-formula (formula 3 in reference [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" doi="10.1016/j.annepidem.2014.11.007" pmid="25511308" count="1">9</citation>] or formula 4 in reference [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" doi="10.1111/j.1541-0420.2005.00355.x" pmid="16135037" count="1">10</citation>].

As PAF is a function of the prevalence of exposure, self-reported measurement of exposures in this study can be lead to bias in the estimation of PAF. <sentence_start/>As reported in this study, the self-reported and local health documentation search of diabetes was not sufficient to estimate the real distribution.

With respect to causal interpretation of PAF in a public health setting, computation of PAF is logical and practical when the exposure is amenable to intervention [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR6" doi="10.2105/AJPH.88.1.15" pmid="9584027" pmcid="PMC1508384" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Therefore, it is less apparent why the attributable fraction for unmodifiable risk factors such as age and sex may be of use.

In sum, unbiased estimation of PAF requires several assumptions which are often ignored in practice. <sentence_start/>We recommend using sample-weighted version of Miettinen formula or sample weighed parametric g-formula [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" doi="10.1136/bmj.k757" pmid="29472187" count="1">3</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR11" doi="10.1136/bmj.j4587" pmid="29038130" count="1">11</citation>].
A.Kh wrote the paper and MA. <sentence_start/>M revised the paper. <sentence_start/>All authors approved the final version of the paper.
